issues.legal_issue: Approved development plans and their amendments held by a public authority are accessible under the right to information regime when they are part of the public approval process and no applicable disclosure exemption is established.
material_facts: The developer had submitted plans, layouts, subdivision plans and amendments to the municipal corporation for approval.
The requested documents were held by the corporation and formed part of its sanction process.
The plans were required to be disclosed to prospective flat purchasers and the law governing real estate development contemplated public access to sanctioned plans.
The requested information was not personal information, and the disclosure of certified copies of the approved plans would not infringe copyright.
The court found that the plans were not commercial secrets or information whose disclosure would harm the developer’s competitive position.
issues.conclusion: The requested approved plans and their amendments had to be disclosed; the claimed exemptions for commercial confidence, intellectual property, personal information and copyright did not justify withholding them.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 2(f) and 2(j) of the Right to Information Act, 2005, information held by or under the control of a public authority includes records and certified copies. Section 74 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, includes public records of private documents among public documents. Disclosure is required unless an exemption under Sections 8 or 9 of the RTI Act applies. Section 8(1)(d) requires commercial confidence, trade secrets or intellectual property to be of a kind whose disclosure would harm a third party’s competitive position, subject to the larger-public-interest exception; Section 8(1)(j) concerns personal information; and Section 9 concerns access that would infringe another person’s copyright. Section 52(1)(f) of the Copyright Act, 1957, excludes from infringement the reproduction of a work in a certified copy made or supplied in accordance with law. The public-disclosure context is supported by Section 3(2)(l) of the Maharashtra Ownership Flats Act, 1963, and Sections 11(1) and 11(3) of the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016. The court considered Thalappalam Service Cooperative Bank Ltd. v. State of Kerala and Dr. V.I. Mathan v. Corporation of Chennai.

rule.if: request_for_public_authority_records and plans_submitted_for_public_approval and plans_required_for_public_disclosure and certified_copies_requested and not personal_private_information and not disclosure_harms_competition

predicates.request_for_public_authority_records: A person requested records held by or under the control of a public authority.
predicates.plans_submitted_for_public_approval: A developer submitted the requested plans and amendments to a public authority as part of obtaining approval for a development.
predicates.plans_required_for_public_disclosure: The plans concerned a development for which the governing framework contemplated making approved plans available to purchasers or the public.
predicates.certified_copies_requested: The applicant requested certified copies of the plans from the public authority.
predicates.personal_private_information: The requested records contain personal information whose disclosure would invade an individual’s privacy.
predicates.disclosure_harms_competition: The requested records are commercial-confidence, trade-secret or intellectual-property information whose disclosure would harm a third party’s competitive position.

issues.definition: When a request concerns certified copies of development plans submitted to a public authority, the plans are required to be publicly disclosed, and neither personal privacy nor competitive harm applies, the approved plans must be disclosed.

issues.legal_issue: A person requesting information held by a public authority need not state a reason or establish a special personal interest, although a larger-public-interest test may apply when an exemption requiring that test is otherwise engaged.
material_facts: The applicant sought information held by the municipal corporation under the statutory information-request procedure.
The appellant argued that the applicant lacked standing and had not shown a larger public interest.
The court held that the request procedure does not require an applicant to provide a reason and that anyone may seek information forming part of a public authority’s records.
The court separately considered whether any claimed exemption applied and found that the requested plans were not exempt.
issues.conclusion: The applicant was not required to establish special standing or give a reason for requesting the information; the absence of a demonstrated larger public interest did not justify withholding these plans because the asserted exemptions did not apply.
issues.legal_principle: Section 6(2) of the Right to Information Act, 2005, provides that a person making a request is not required to give reasons for seeking information. Sections 8(1)(d) and 8(1)(j) permit disclosure in larger public interest where their respective exemptions apply. In Thalappalam Service Cooperative Bank Ltd. v. State of Kerala, the court considered the public-interest test for exempt information; here, it held that the test arose only if an exemption was engaged.

predicates.public_information_request: A person made a request for information through the statutory public-information procedure.
predicates.information_held_by_public_authority: The requested information was held by or under the control of a public authority.
predicates.requester_seeks_public_record: The requester sought information forming part of a public authority’s records.

issues.definition: When a person seeks a public record held by a public authority through the information-request procedure, that person need not state a reason or establish a special interest.

issues.legal_issue: A prior civil proceeding does not bar a separate information request where the information sought is different and the earlier proceeding did not adjudicate the request for that information on its merits.
material_facts: The applicant had earlier sought documents in an interim-relief application in a civil suit between the parties.
The earlier documents included a broader set of materials, while the later information request specifically sought approved plans and their modifications held by the municipal corporation.
The earlier courts had not adjudicated the request for those plans; their decisions concerned other issues, including a preliminary jurisdictional issue.
The applicant later sought the plans through the independent statutory information-request procedure.
issues.conclusion: The prior civil proceeding did not bar the information request, and the objections based on issue estoppel, constructive res judicata or election of remedy were rejected.
issues.legal_principle: The court found no basis to apply issue estoppel, constructive res judicata or election of remedy because the information sought under the Right to Information Act, 2005, differed from the earlier request and the earlier proceeding had not adjudicated this disclosure issue. The Act creates an independent right to seek information, distinct from the parties’ inter se rights in civil litigation.

rule.if: information_request_proceeding and earlier_civil_document_request and information_requests_differ and earlier_court_did_not_decide_disclosure_merits

predicates.information_request_proceeding: A person pursued a request for public records through the statutory information-request procedure.
predicates.earlier_civil_document_request: The same requester had earlier sought documents in a civil proceeding.
predicates.information_requests_differ: The records sought through the information-request procedure were different from the documents sought in the civil proceeding.
predicates.earlier_court_did_not_decide_disclosure_: The earlier court proceedings did not decide on the merits whether the later-requested records had to be disclosed.

issues.definition: When a statutory information request seeks different records from an earlier civil document request that was not decided on its merits, the earlier civil proceeding does not bar the information request.

issues.legal_issue: Severability does not restrict disclosure when the requested information contains no exempt material, and a third party’s objection does not prevent disclosure after that party has been given an opportunity to object.
material_facts: The developer and its architect were permitted to object to disclosure, and their objections were considered by the information authorities.
The court found that the requested plans did not fall within the relevant disclosure exemptions.
The developer argued that only permission or approval documents, rather than the underlying plans, could be disclosed.
issues.conclusion: The provisions concerning severability and third-party consultation did not prevent disclosure of the plans.
issues.legal_principle: Section 10 of the Right to Information Act, 2005, permits severance where part of requested information is exempt, but requires protected material to exist in the information sought. Section 11 provides a third party an opportunity to make submissions about disclosure; that procedure was complied with when the developer and architect were allowed to object and their objections were considered.

predicates.public_information_request: A person requested records through the statutory public-information procedure.
predicates.no_exempt_material_in_requested_records: The requested records contain no information protected by a disclosure exemption.
predicates.third_party_given_opportunity_to_object: A third party whose information was involved was allowed to object, and the objection was considered.

issues.definition: When requested records contain no exempt material and an affected third party has had an opportunity to object, severability and third-party consultation do not bar disclosure.

issues.legal_issue: Sanctioned plans and layout plans for a development should be displayed at the development site to promote transparency and address violations.
material_facts: The dispute concerned development plans approved by a public authority.
The court noted the requirement that sanctioned plans and layout plans be made available to allottees and the importance of transparency.
The court considered the ground reality of rampant violations and the consequences of those violations.
issues.conclusion: The court stated that developers should display sanctioned plans and layout plans at the site, in addition to any other manner prescribed by regulations, and that this position should receive appropriate publicity as part of enforcement.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11(3) of the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016, requires promoters to make sanctioned plans, layout plans and specifications available to allottees by display at the site or another place specified by regulations. The court also referred to Dr. V.I. Mathan v. Corporation of Chennai in support of public access to sanctioned plans.

predicates.development_project_has_approved_plans: A developer has obtained approval for plans or layout plans for a development project.
predicates.project_plans_concern_public_transparenc: Making the approved plans accessible at the project would promote transparency about the development.

issues.definition: When a development project has approved plans whose accessibility promotes transparency, those plans should be displayed at the project site.
